title: Cultural Identity, Assumptions, and the Meaning of Normal
before: How learned expectations about time, family, communication and work become familiar standards, and how to keep them open to evidence.

turns.text: Cultural Identity, Assumptions, and the Meaning of Normal looks at something we rarely question: the sense that our own way of doing things is simply normal. Culture is learned, varied, and always changing, and that includes professional and workplace cultures. This course follows how those cultures shape assumptions in DSD services, forms, recruitment, and everyday teamwork.

It begins with a welcome, where a host offers everyone a shared meal, and one person declines and asks to sit nearby instead. It would be easy to decide that person is unfriendly. The course asks you to separate what was observed from what came from the host’s own expectation, which turns out to be a useful habit far beyond meals.

The course then moves into our own work, where a service form asks for “the household decision-maker.” The person says they make their own choices and want support with one topic. The form has already assumed an answer about how decisions are made. You will practice deciding what staff should clarify, without letting the form or a community brief settle it for them.

Part of what the course does is show how professional culture has defaults too. Terms, meeting habits, and ideas about what a strong contribution looks like feel obvious inside a profession. To a newcomer or a community participant, they can arrive as unexplained requirements. The course keeps expertise in place while asking that the route to participation be understandable.

I found the example about flattering predictions helpful. “Younger staff are naturally good with technology” sounds positive, but it does not establish skill or interest. Automatic assignments built on it can add unwanted work for some people and limit learning for others. A compliment can still be a stereotype when it decides who gets which work.

Recruitment has a similar trap, where a candidate is praised as a good fit because they share the team’s hobbies and conversational style. Those similarities can feel comfortable without showing readiness for the job. You will practice improving that comparison, and the course also notices how a casual preference carries more weight when it comes from someone who assigns work or reviews performance.

Then the course takes on group evidence, which is subtle. A group-level pattern can identify a real equity question without predicting any one person. So you keep the population, the time, and the missing information visible. A community brief offers context, but it cannot tell you an individual’s view, and Native American and Tribal-specific matters stay within referral guidance.

One practice case brings that together when several participants find an appointment instruction confusing, and a draft says the whole community cannot understand policy. The draft has turned a concern about an instruction into a claim about people. You will consider which revision respects the evidence and keeps the access question open without attaching a group label to it.

Toward the end, you rewrite a familiar expectation like “good fit,” “naturally skilled,” or “not interested.” You replace it with the relevant task, the observed evidence, and a question still open. The course also points out that recognizing an assumption is real learning, even when the form or criterion it shaped still needs review through the right responsibility.

As you begin, think about one expectation in your own work that feels completely normal to you, perhaps about how quickly people respond, how meetings run, or who speaks for a household. Where did that expectation come from? Keep it in mind, because the course will give you a way to check whether it describes the work or only describes what is familiar.

guidance.title: Several affiliations at once
guidance.text: Culture includes meanings and practices people learn through relationships, language, place, professions, and communities. Because everyone holds several affiliations, and because meaning can shift across settings and over time, a single identity cannot tell you someone’s preferences, abilities, or beliefs. That is not a reason to ignore culture. It is a reason to ask, and to let the person’s answer carry more weight than the category.

guidance.title: Testing a familiar default
guidance.text: Return to the expectation you rewrote. In your own work, has a similar expectation shaped a form, a criterion, or who gets an assignment? If it has, what responsibility would govern its review, and who holds it? Consider what evidence would show that an alternative actually improved the choice or opportunity at issue, rather than only sounding more inclusive.
